content.summary_of_the_paper: The sensitive dependence on initial conditions and parametric values makes a time series generated from a chaotic dynamical system affect the generalizability of a time series classification algorithm. In this work, the authors improve the generalizability of a Multivariate LSTM Fully Convolution Network (MLSTM FCN) by applying time series decomposition and extracting residual components  from time series to train the model. The dynamical system used to generate the data is the oscillating electric arc RLC circuit (3D coupled differential equations), which exhibits chaotic and periodic for various values of R, C and L. The authors have formulated a binary classification problem, for the classification of chaotic and periodic time series. In the second set of experiments, the authors use clustering algorithms like Kmeans, Gaussian Mixture Models,  and OPTICS algorithms for chaotic and periodic time series classification. The authors compare and contrast the results obtained using MLSTM FCN (with residual component - trained using residual component) and MLSTM FCN (without residual component). From the results, it can be seen that MLSTM FCN (without residual component, F1-score = 96.28) slightly outperforms MLSTM FCN (with residual component, F1-score = 95.82). However, they subsequently show that MLSTM FCN (without residual component) is sensitive to values of R, C and L used in the training set. If the R, C and L are perturbed, the performance degrades. Whereas the extent degradation in the performance is less when MLSTM FCN is trained with residual components.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The strength of the paper is that the authors have showcased robust features of chaotic time series classification (time series decomposition and residual components extracted from time series). 

The weakness of the paper is in relation to the set of experiments carried out. In my opinion chaotic vs periodic classification is an easier problem. The real test of this algorithm will be in the classification of a chaotic and random time series. Classification of chaotic and random time series data will provide better insight about the efficacy of the feature and the model. Even though a chaotic dynamical system is deterministic, the time series generated from the chaotic dynamical system looks random.I would like to see the performance of the  MLSTM FCN on the classification of chaotic and random time series data.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity

In my opinion, there are issues with the flow and connectivity of ideas in the paper . Section 2.2 can be improved. The following questions can be addressed:

Are the residual components equal to the number of local maxima in the projected timeseries to XY plane?

What is the significance of the method mentioned in Marszalek et al. (2019). The authors have used this method but the intuition and benefit of this method is not discussed.

What is the rationale behind the assumption - identification process of periodic responses was done up to the number of local maximum points equal to 22.


What is the role of the periodogram averaging method described in section 2.3? I feel there is an issue with the flow of ideas in this manuscript. The authors can concretely mention what exactly is the input to the model. 

Justification for the following is required: if the mean > 2 we classified all time-series in a cluster as a chaotic time-series, otherwise we classified them as periodic responses. 
Why mean > 2?

Can this idea be used in concept drift problems?


Quality

In my opinion, the flow of the ideas in the paper can be improved. The experimental results are convincing. However, the authors can comment on the classification of random and chaotic time series using the MLSTM FCN Residual Network.

 Novelty 

The authors have shown robustness of MLSTM FCN model when trained with residual components. It seems like this idea in principle can be applied to general time series classification problems.


Reproducibility: Seems reproducible
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall the paper addresses a robust set of features for chaotic time series classification. The experiment set up can be improved by adding a more challenging set of problems - like classification of chaotic and random time series. The flow of the manuscript can be further improved. (Borderline Paper).

content.summary_of_the_paper: If I understood correctly, this paper deals with the classification of time series into ‘periodic’ vs. ‘chaotic’. An artificial (simulated) dataset of periodic and chaotic time series is created from a 3d ODE system (RLC). Some numbers are obtained from the time series (similar to a Poincaré section) to decide whether they are periodic or chaotic. A specific neural network (LSTM-FCN) as well as different clustering approaches are applied to the data to infer whether a given stretch of time series came from a periodic or a chaotic system. This is done before and after removing components such as trend and seasonality (= residual).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is quite poorly and confusingly presented, with little to no formal detail, so it might well be that I missed some points. It was somewhat hard to understand what the authors exactly did and why.

To be honest, I don’t even understand the problem tackled: If all this is just to decide whether a system with known equations is periodic or chaotic, then the Lyapunov spectrum computed from the system’s known Jacobians is the standard, easy, and quick way to go (or some Poincaré based technique as used by the authors). 
If it is, however, to develop a technique that also works for real world data, then:
- No real world data were considered in this paper.
- Not anything close to a real world scenario (with noise, high-dimensional, partially observed etc.) was simulated.
- For empirically recorded time series there are also many simple techniques and statistical tests available that have been developed over the past decades (see famous textbooks by Kantz & Schreiber or Abarbanel for a start). In real-world situations, the differentiation between chaotic and periodic-noisy time series is actually statistically tricky.
- The introduced ‘method’ of working on the residuals after subtracting off components like trend or oscillations to ease the detection of chaos is fairly commonplace (textbook essentially) in the fields of time series analysis and nonlinear dynamics, nothing novel here.

The paper is quite thin in many respects: Just *one* simulated and no real dataset considered (compared to the usually 5-10 datasets considered in other papers dealing with dynamical systems questions). It is, for instance, entirely unclear whether the simple classifier approach based on mean \& variance would work for other systems, let alone in an empirically relevant situation. Just *one* RNN method of unclear origin and motivation is considered (dynamical systems is a currently hugely expanding field in ML, there are easily 10 SOTA methods not even mentioned).
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper is relatively poorly presented, and addresses a problem of unclear relevance. Much of the existing literature is not covered. As far as I could see, none of the methods are novel (but in fact rather standard). Evaluation on just one simulated dataset under not too realistic assumptions is by far not sufficient.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 1: The contributions are neither significant nor novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper demonstrated that the time-series decomposition helps in the improvement of the classification abilities of the MLTSM-FCN neural networks. It was illustrated that the residual components transfer most of the information about the chaotic behavior of the dynamical system, as the clustering algorithms could extrapolate a lot of features of the bifurcation diagram without prior knowledge of either of the dynamical system itself or labels.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strength**

The core idea of the paper is nice and interesting. 

**Weaknesses**

1) In dynamical systems theory, a bifurcation diagram shows the possible long-term values (equilibria/fixed points or periodic orbits or chaotic attractors) of a system as a function of a bifurcation parameter in the system. Please see the following references:

Strogatz, S.H. (1994) Nonlinear Dynamics and Chaos: With Application to Physics, Biology, Chemistry and Engineering. Perseus Books Publishing, Cambridge.

 Perko, L. (2001) Differential Equations and Dynamical Systems. 3rd Edition, Springer-Verlag.
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4613-0003-8

So, technically, the diagrams plotted in figures 4 and 5 are not bifurcation diagrams. They are usually called the "stability diagram" or we can simply call them "two-parameter bifurcations". Please see  page 71 of Strogatz book; and also the following paper:

Gallas, J.A.C. Stability diagrams for a memristor oscillator. Eur. Phys. J. Spec. Top. 228, 2081–2091 (2019). https://doi.org/10.1140/epjst/e2019-900009-8

2) How can we ensure the time series in figure 1 (a) is chaotic? It could be also a quasi-periodic time series. Moreover, on page 5, it is mentioned that "If a response was identified as not being periodic, then such a response was classified as a chaotic". A trajectory, however, is not necessarily chaotic if it is not periodic. Actually, an aperiodic trajectory could be *chaotic* or *quasi-periodic*. The last sentence of page 5 is not true either. A time series cannot be classified as periodic, if it is not chaotic.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper is about chaotic time-series classification. The proposed method improves the generalization ability of the multivariate LSTM-FCN model by extracting the training the model on the residual component of the time-series. The results show that by taking the mean and variance of the residual component, the model extracts many very interesting features of the 2D bifurcation diagrams using the K-Means, GMM and OPTICS clustering algorithms.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- This paper is about an interesting topic: time-series classification. Specifically, they study chaotic time-series.
- Even though, there is no related work in the paper, the authors mention the related works mostly in the introduction and methodology sections, and they seem to cover a decent amount of them.
- The authors use an interesting dataset.
- The proposed methodology has potential and the results are promising. 

Weaknesses:
- This paper might not be a good fit for ICLR. I would suggest a more applied track or a journal with larger page limit so that the authors can dive more into the details of the proposed methodology and add more results to support better their contributions.
- The paper is hard to follow. The structure of the paper is not very clear and makes it hard for the reader to understand the motivation, the challenges, the existing works, the methodology and the results/discussion. It would be useful to add a figure with the overview of the methodology, and then one by one for each component to have an analysis of the existing work and challenges, and how it is used in a different way in this model. There is a specific use case/dataset that we follow along the whole paper, I would suggest to dedicate a sub-section/paragraph to describe the dataset, the dataset stats and its particularities.
- The contributions and the novelty of this work are not clear. I would suggest to add a contributions paragraph on the introduction section, as well as highlight them when describing each part in the methodology section. The novelty of this work is limited. The authors rely a lot on existing methodology, and because the writing is not very clear, it makes it hard to identify the contributions and the novelty.
- In the results section there is no clear comparison of the MLSTM-FCN model and the three comparison models. It would be useful for the reader if the authors could move the figures and tables for them to appear in the pages that those are mentioned, so that they do not appear in the last pages of the paper after the conclusion section. 

Minor Comment:
- In the introduction it would be useful to add references and links to the well known systems that are being mentioned.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: I have made some comments and suggestions in the weaknesses section above. The writing style and the structure of the paper needs more work to improve clarity and justification of the methodology and the use of each component. The novelty and the contributions of this work are limited and not very clear. They need to be emphasized more in the future version of this paper. The code and data are provided in the supplementary material.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, I find it hard to follow this work. The structure of the paper is not helping. Some suggestions are made in the weaknesses. The novelty and the contributions of the paper are not emphasized and they look limited. The results section can also be improved by increasing the discussion for the results, for example for the figures that are obtained from the clustering.
